I'm going to tell you what, and he and my brother play in Chicago. My little grandchild had that first deliverance over the keys, you know. Sounds so much like jelly, and you'd be surprised at the resemblance. Wait, let me show you his picture.
Yes, um—

My—my grandson's picture. I have these two large pictures that look just like— Of your grandson. My grandson. Look like more than my son did. Oh, yeah. When he was a little boy. It's a nice picture. And I have nothing to be proud of him because he's never given me a day's trouble. What kind of a piano did your brother have in Chicago? A baby grand. A baby grand. A baby grand. A baby grand. Well, I was going to ask some more about that visit in Chicago, because that's the longest time that you knew your brother during that year. But you know what?

Yes.

Yes. Oh, there's one thing you told about, as I say, I didn't see that program on television, but I did hear the tape of it. Mm-hmm. And I remember you told him when you were ready to go, you stood, I think you stood up at the...

When did you... that was Victor Koloss. Yeah, Koloss. Is that what you pronounce the name? Yes, Koloss. He looked just like a Frenchman, too.

My grandmother, too, looked just like him. That's why those kids all looked alike. In fact, my sister had so much light blood behind her, she didn't have a dark child. She's the only one that came out dark, and she blamed my mother for it, too. She never did forgive her for that, she said.
Well, you shouldn't hold that.
God made you one. I used to tell her all the time. I said, you don't believe in God if you think mother had anything to do with that. Yeah, that's right. Nobody knows.
Did you say after your grandmother, you were telling your grandfather Creole and your grandmother white, or how was it?

No, I wouldn't either. Portuguese names would be hard to spell.

Well, I don't—you know, I put Francis M. Oliver all the time. And the M's can either be for Mimi or Mouton. That's what I thought it was for the Mouton. Yes, it is for the Mouton. Because I never have dropped my father's name. Yes.

Right at home. Midwives, you know. What? Granny women, he called them. Yeah. Thank you. Um, you went to school at a Catholic school? Yes. I understand. I hate to keep just annoying with all those questions, but I just thought in case you'd heard somebody else say something about the—

Yes. Because the first name, because I wasn't the—I tried to guess at the name like that. I may not use that material either, but in case—I did want to mention what the grandmother—

That's right. After all, there's so few people can go back to the first generation. Can go back and tell that family. The family history, that's right. And my grandmother—my great-grandmother died in 1913. 1913. And mind you, I was in the bed with her. She had an abscess on the liver. The two of them were there. They were staying at night with her, but I slept with her. Yes. And I remember when this abscess burst, and when the blood and all this came out through her mouth, she—and she was dead. She didn't say another word after that. And your older sister, just maybe a couple years older than you, you think, through your
fours? That's all. About four, I think. I know, because she won't tell me. Yes, she won't tell. No.
Mm-hmm. So, um—and then your grandmother's name was Laura.

But I mean, they call her Laura, but her name was Eleonora—Eleanor, just like Eleanor Roosevelt. Eleanor. Just like Ele—just like Eleanor Roosevelt. Eleanor? Just like Ele—just like Eleanor Roosevelt.
Eleanor Roosevelt. Her name is really good. Yes, indeed. And she married—
She married Neville Monette. Neville. No, wait, no, she married—I'm—not Neville, his name was Julian. J-U-L-I-E-N, a hyphen over the E, because I have my mother's marriage license here.

Yes. Julian Monette. That's where my son gets his name from. And Laura was the grandmother. Grandmother. And then your mother—
My mother was named Louise. Louise. Monette. Yes, Monette. And she married first, uh, Le Monde—M-O-N-T-H-E.

That's right. Yeah. And then she married Mouton. Was it Le Monde—L-E or L-A? It's L-A. L-A. And it's a small L-A for Le Monde. The Monde is coming from the capital L. Yes. Because all friends' names are small— Yes. —that is to begin with. Mm-hmm.
L-A—L-A.
The names of the family.

The names of the family. The names of the family. I think we got it all right. About your mother, uh, Louise Monette. Mm-hmm. And married L-A-M-O-N-T-H-E. L-A. The little L-A. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
She died a year I was born.

A-M-I-D-E.
A-M-I.

It's French, French, pre-all from downtown? Yeah, Arcadia, France. Yeah, from Arcadia. Not from here, from Arcadia County. Oh, Arcadia.
That's right. You came from out- Yes, uh-huh. Is that west of here, like near the- New Liberia or-

I don't know anything about small towns in Louisiana, real and truly. I can tell you all about Texas, because my husband and I used to travel out in Texas. But here, I mean, we didn't go anywhere. My aunts, you know, my uncle's wives. I have one aunt that's living in Berkeley, California, where my uncle Gus just died here about three years ago, and she's nearly 80 herself. Yeah.
That was by- she was by Mary. Yes, that would be by Mary.

That's right.

And my son writes music beautifully, too. My son saxophonically. He writes music. He wrote—he wrote out a little song for—a little number for my grandson the other day to play on the piano. It really sounds good.

Yes, uh-huh. So he could evidently read it very well then, that's how he learned to read it and could write it. That's right, that's right.

And I thought my son was going to be just like him because he's a wonderful saxophonist, and he plays clarinet, too. in Louisiana a long time ago, people believed in class and caste, you know. I guess, yeah, that's right. They say some of the late CREOs, you know, didn't want to...

So you were only 25 then. That's right.

That's right. And he was so particular about his teeth, he had two or three of them, caps. Now that I know what it means, we said white caps on them, you know what I mean?
